title: Maj. Joseph Bowman
summary: Joseph Bowman, George Rogers Clark's second-in-command in 1778–1779, kept a journal of the march to Vincennes and was the only American officer to die.
bodyMarkdown:
Joseph Bowman, an early Kentucky settler, was George Rogers Clark's second-in-command in the 1778–1779 campaign for the Illinois Country. According to William H. English's history of the campaign, he was the only American officer to die in the 1778–1779 Illinois campaign. His daily journal of the winter march to Vincennes is one of the best firsthand accounts of it.

## A Kentucky settler

An account of [Joseph Bowman](https://grokipedia.com/page/joseph_bowman) says he was born around 1752 in Frederick County, Virginia, a son of George Bowman and Mary Hite. He served in the Virginia militia in Lord Dunmore's War in 1774 and moved to Kentucky the next year.

In 1776 he was among the Harrodsburg petitioners seeking a new county. On September 11, 1777, thirty-seven men gathered at his place to shell corn and were attacked by Native warriors. One settler was killed and six wounded before the attackers withdrew.

Joseph is sometimes confused with his brother, [Colonel John Bowman](/stories/col-john-bowman-at-old-chillicothe/), who led the 1779 raid on Old Chillicothe.

## With Clark in the Illinois Country

In early 1778 [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/) offered Bowman a commission if he could raise a company. Bowman joined Clark's force on May 12, 1778, and was at the capture of Fort Gage at Kaskaskia on July 4.

He then led a mixed force of Virginians, local residents and French Canadians north to take Prairie du Rocher, Fort de Chartres and Cahokia. He commanded at Cahokia for a time, at a post renamed Fort Bowman.

## The march to Vincennes

British Lieutenant Governor Henry Hamilton retook Vincennes late in 1778. In February 1779, Bowman marched with Clark about 180 miles to besiege the fort and took part in the surrender talks. After Hamilton [surrendered Fort Sackville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege_of_Fort_Vincennes) in late February 1779, Clark raised the American flag and renamed it Fort Patrick Henry.

Within days, a dispatch arrived promoting Clark to general and Bowman to major. Bowman was later granted 4,312 acres in Clark's Grant north of the Ohio.

## A fatal salute

On February 25, 1779, a cannon salute celebrated the victory. Some powder charges ignited by accident, wounding several men and burning Bowman critically. Clark's memoir never mentions the accident and describes Bowman leading soldiers as late as June.

Bowman's health failed from his burns, and he died at Fort Patrick Henry in August 1779. One account gives August 14, while another, a cited history, says he probably died on August 15 and was buried on August 18.

## Kentucky today

Bowman's grave marker stands at St. Francis Xavier Cathedral Cemetery in Vincennes, Indiana, near George Rogers Clark National Historical Park. In Kentucky, the family name lived on through his brothers. An account of [John Bowman](https://grokipedia.com/page/john_bowman_%28pioneer%29) notes that their grandnephew John Bryan Bowman founded Kentucky University and the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Kentucky. Joseph's journal remains a key source for historians of the campaign, and his funeral was recreated at the 2006 Spirit of Vincennes Rendezvous.
